readerTitle: Why Apple let strangers build on its best product
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Apple, 2007~2009년 App Store 개방) + 일화 (잡스의 초기 반대, Isaacson 전기) + 가상 적용 (아웃도어 용품 소매 체인)
insight: Apple의 선택은 '열 것인가 닫을 것인가'가 아니었다. 문은 열되 관문은 지켰다. 남이 만든 보완재가 핵심 제품의 가치를 키우고, 관문의 규칙과 수수료로 그 가치의 일부를 회수했다.
misconception: 최고의 제품은 회사가 직접 모든 것을 만들어야 품질과 수익을 지킬 수 있다. 외부에 여는 순간 통제권을 잃는다.

sources.text: Apple Newsroom: iPhone 출시 (2007년 6월), iPhone SDK 발표 (2008년 3월), App Store 출시 (2008년 7월 10일)
Apple Newsroom (2009년 4월): App Store 10억 다운로드 달성
Isaacson, W. (2011). Steve Jobs. Simon & Schuster. (잡스가 처음에는 외부 앱에 반대했다는 서술)
Apple Developer Program 안내 (연 $99, 70/30 수익 배분), Apple Newsroom (2020년 11월) App Store Small Business Program 발표
Epic Games v. Apple (미국, 2020년 제소), EU Digital Markets Act 관련 Apple 발표 (2024)

factChecks.note: iPhone은 2007년 6월 29일 미국 출시 당시 외부 개발자의 네이티브 앱을 설치할 수 없었고, Apple은 웹 앱을 대안으로 제시했습니다. 게시 전 Apple 보도자료로 확인하세요.
SDK 공개 2008년 3월, App Store 출시 2008년 7월 10일, 출시 당시 앱 약 500개. Apple 보도자료 기준. 카드에는 'about 500'으로 적었습니다.
10억 다운로드는 2009년 4월 Apple 발표 기준이며, 출시 후 약 9개월입니다. 카드에는 'less than a year'로 적었습니다.
잡스가 처음에 외부 앱에 반대했고 이사회 멤버 등이 설득했다는 이야기는 Isaacson 전기의 서술입니다. 카드에서 'reportedly'로 일화임을 표시했습니다.
수익 배분 70/30, 개발자 프로그램 연 $99는 출시 당시 기준입니다. 소규모 개발자 15% 인하(Small Business Program)는 2020년 11월 발표, 2021년 1월 시행. Epic 소송(2020)과 EU DMA(2024년 적용) 관련 서술은 일반적인 수준으로만 적었습니다. 특정 국가의 법률 해석은 담지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Apple let strangers build on its best product
body: When the iPhone went on sale in June 2007, it came only with Apple's own apps. Outside developers couldn't install anything on it.
A year later, Apple opened a store where almost anyone could sell software for the phone. That decision changed what the iPhone was.

image.label: An early smartphone with only a few app icons on its screen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 화면에 아이콘이 몇 개뿐인 단순한 스마트폰. 옆에 빈 진열대가 있고 문이 살짝 열려 빛이 들어옴. 실제 Apple 로고, 아이콘, 제품 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's late 2007. Do you let outsiders in?
body: You make a hit phone. Developers are begging to build apps for it. Some are already hacking the phone to install their own.
Opening up could bring buggy or harmful software onto a device you've carefully controlled. What do you do?

options.text: Stay closed. Developers can build web apps that run in the browser
options.feedback: You keep full control of quality and security. But web apps of that era couldn't do much, so you limit the phone to what your own team can imagine.

options.text: Open fully. Anyone can install any software, like on a PC
options.feedback: You get the most apps fastest. But you lose any say over quality and safety, and you earn nothing from the software others sell.

options.text: Open through one store you run, with app review and a share of sales
options.feedback: You gain outside creativity while keeping a gate. The cost: you now have to review thousands of apps and manage developers who may resent your rules.

cards.title: Apple opened the door, but kept a gate.
body: Steve Jobs reportedly resisted outside apps at first, and colleagues argued him around. In March 2008, Apple released a kit for developers. In July 2008, the **App Store** opened with about 500 apps.
Every app went through Apple's review. Apple handled hosting, payments and distribution. Developers kept 70% of each sale, and free apps were distributed free.
It was neither closed nor fully open. It was open on Apple's terms.

cards.title: Complements turned a product into a platform.
body: A **complement** is something that makes another product more valuable. Apps are complements to a phone.

Before the store, the iPhone was worth what Apple built into it. After, it was worth what thousands of outside developers built too: games, maps, banking, tools Apple would never have thought to make.
Apple stopped selling just a product and started running a **platform**: a base others build on.

image.label: A phone at the center with many outside app makers connected to it
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 스마트폰, 주변에 다양한 개발자(게임, 지도, 은행, 음악 등 직업을 나타내는 작은 인물)가 화살표로 연결. 폰과 개발자 사이에 'Review gate' 표지가 있는 작은 문. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: How the store split the value.
body: Developers got customers and payments without building their own stores. Apple got a share of sales and a reason for people to buy its phone.

cards.title: Each side pulled in the other.
body: More iPhone owners meant more customers for developers. More apps gave people more reasons to buy an iPhone. The store passed one billion downloads in less than a year.
Apple didn't need to predict which apps people wanted. It only needed to make building them easy and selling them worthwhile.
cards.softwareNote: Any software product with an API or plugin system faces the same choice. Outside add-ons can make your core product far more useful than your own roadmap could, if you make them easy to build and worth building.

cards.title: A gate earns money, and resentment.
body: The rules that protect quality also give the gatekeeper power over everyone inside. Over time, many developers complained about the 30% share and unclear rejections.
Apple later cut its rate to 15% for smaller developers. In 2020, Epic Games sued Apple over its store rules, and EU law has since pushed Apple to allow other ways to install apps.
Controlling the gate is valuable. It also invites pushback once outsiders depend on you.

cards.title: Now it's an outdoor-gear store.
body: You run five outdoor-gear stores and a website. Customers keep asking for niche items you don't stock: handmade knives, local trail maps, specialty climbing gear.
Small makers want to sell through you. What do you do?

options.text: Keep buying and stocking everything yourself
options.feedback: You control quality fully, but you carry the inventory risk and only offer what your buyers think of. The long list of niche requests stays unmet.

options.text: Let outside makers list on your site, with quality standards and a commission
options.feedback: Makers add range you couldn't build alone, and the commission pays for your effort. You'll need to enforce standards and treat makers fairly to keep them.

options.text: Let any maker list anything, no checks, no fee
options.feedback: You get range fast, but one bad product hurts your name, and you earn nothing from the traffic you bring.

cards.title: Open the door, keep the gate.
body: Outsiders can make your product worth far more than you could alone. Set the terms so quality holds and you share in the value.
**Try it today:** list three things customers ask for that you don't offer. Could an outside partner provide one on your terms?
